note_out: Page ties the intelligence explosion to existential risk and AI-alignment research (MIRI, FHI).
Described as a work of materialist philosophy; La Mettrie is part of the tradition rather than a source of modern physicalism.
SEP: functionalism is officially neutral between materialism and dualism, though attractive to materialists; arose as an alternative to identity theory. 'Builds' is a judgement.
Turing machines inspired Putnam's machine functionalism; sources do not derive multiple realisability from universal computation specifically.
Argument is explicitly directed against functionalism and computationalism.
Block's China brain and inverted qualia objections; this is his 1978 work, not the 1995 access/phenomenal paper.
Dennett calls himself a 'teleofunctionalist' in Consciousness Explained.
Functional explanation leaves experience unexplained; Chalmers targets reductive functionalism only.
Paper's title and abstract state it; Thagard says substrate independence fails in important real cases, not always.
Seth challenges computational functionalism and argues consciousness depends on our nature as living organisms.
Abstract offers a 'physically grounded refutation of computational functionalism'.
Symposium paper: Chirimuuta argues against the literal interpretation of computational models; target is computationalism in neuroscience more than functionalism generally.
Seth credits Searle with biological naturalism but says he uses the term in a slightly different way.
Chalmers uses Nagel's 'what it is like' definition of consciousness.
Nagel's paper is often cited in qualia debates, though it does not use the word 'qualia'.
Levine's explanatory gap argument is presented as an argument about qualia.
Bridging the explanatory gap 'is known as the hard problem'.
Sources name Leibniz's mill as a precursor of the hard problem; none says Chalmers drew on it. 'Related' would be documented.
Leibniz's mill is listed as a precursor argument to the Chinese room.
Interest in the hard problem revived panpsychism; Chalmers himself explored it.
New mysterianism (McGinn) is treated as one response to the hard problem.
Frankish: 'the hard problem is replaced by the illusion problem'.
Frankish coins the term and names Dennett as illusionism's pre-eminent defender.
In The Conscious Mind (1996) Chalmers calls Dennett's position a denial of consciousness.
They co-edited The Mind's I (1981).
Gödel's self-referential construction is Hofstadter's prototypical strange loop.
Penrose argued from Gödel's theorem to non-computability of mind; the argument is widely criticised.
Penrose and Hameroff section discusses quantum coherence in microtubules and includes a quote contrasting them with nerve signals as quantum-computer material.
Link is biographical: Koch moved from NCC work with Crick to collaborating with Tononi. IIT itself did not grow out of NCC research.
Crick and Koch (1990) tied binding to visual awareness via synchronous 40 Hz oscillations.
Aaronson showed simple arrangements of logic gates would have unboundedly high phi.
Abstract: the approach 'generalizes Giulio Tononi's integrated information framework' to arbitrary quantum systems.
Chalmers and Searle consider IIT a form of panpsychism; Tononi and Koch accept only some elements.
Paper says the prior is inspired by and anchored on global workspace theory.
Global workspace theory is one of the theories from which indicator properties are derived.
Computational higher-order theories are among the theories surveyed.
Graziano et al. argue AST and HOT are interlocking perspectives on the same mechanism.
Baars describes the brain in GWT as a 'society of mind' (Minsky's phrase) without naming Minsky; no page states the link outright.
Essay compares both dual-process views and notes Kahneman studied Freud; Freud's repressed unconscious differs from System 1.
Page says the rider and elephant metaphor corresponds to Systems 2 and 1.
Seth builds his case on predictive processing and the free energy principle; 'beast machines' phrase is used.
Seth (2013) says his model is related to Damasio's, both grounding selfhood in physiological condition; his adds top-down inference.
Damasio 'recovered William James' perspective on feelings as a read-out of body states' and expanded it.
Fields, Friston, Glazebrook and Levin reformulate the free energy principle for generic quantum systems (2022, later than the point's 2012 date).
Levin's publication list shows more than a dozen Fields and Levin papers since 2018.
The concept played a central role in Westworld; season 1 finale is titled 'The Bicameral Mind'.
Commentators read conscious realism as idealism, but Hoffman writes that his interface theory 'is not idealism' and distances conscious realism from Kant.
Metzinger's claim concerns the self, not phenomenal properties; Frankish's founding paper does not discuss him. Thematic parallel only.
Kegan places his work in the constructive-developmental tradition that includes Piaget.
Leary read the book in 1960 and then met Huxley; the specific 'filtered mind' idea in Leary is not sourced.
Both appear as separate quantum approaches to mind on the same page; no influence between them is claimed.
Seth draws on autopoiesis (Maturana and Varela) and cites enactive and 4E work as allied to his view.
The Matrix popularised the idea of humans unknowingly living in a machine-generated reality.
Article on the simulation argument discusses Permutation City as an exploration of living as a copy in a simulated world.
Blindsight treats consciousness as real but dispensable, which differs from illusionism; Watts's own notes cite Metzinger, and the novel predates the term.
